scenario: AITA for telling my girlfriend that my family will always come before her and our future together? | My girlfriend expects me to build a future for us. A little back story: She's a student right now and works part time but barely makes enough to pay her rent/school fees. I'm 24 and work a minimum wage + commission job, I have barely any money saved so she doesn't understand why I spend so much money/time with family We've been dating 3 years with no problems except for this, we love each other and live independent lives but she worries that I'm too focused on helping my family and making them happy instead of building a future for us. She's working as much as she can to pay her bills but because shes a student and also doing her required interning she can't work much more. She doesnt ever ask me for money to help her right now because she wants me to save up. She doesn't have a family like mine so she doesn't understand, my family is close and I really want to take care of them. She says that I'm supposed to be worrying about my own future right now. She says that she doesn't understand because my mom recently received about ~100k for a settlement and bought a house and a new car and I shouldn't be worrying about helping when they seem fine. She is angry that I dont take my life seriously, I've been trying to get my real estate license for a few months now but cant find the time to study because of how demanding my family is, they get really angry/sad when I'm not around for family events and I understand why, we're a close family. I get where shes coming from but I cant drop my family. I told her all of this and she got angry saying that shes not asking me to abandon my family, she just wants to make sure we have a solid foundation before we worry about helping my family. And I cant build a future if I'm always with them. She expects me to start saving up money for a downpayment on a house while she finishes and gets her degree and can start helping as well but I keep telling her my family needs me first. We had a particularly heated fight, the worst we've ever had last night and she said she feels like I'll never care enough about my future and I'm supposed to be building one for myself and her and she can't be with someone like that. She said if I really feel like helping my family comes before my own future than that is my choice but she's going to have no choice but to worry about herself from now on and plan a future where shes her only priority because I make it sound like I don't want to be part of it. Shes stopped mentioning anything about it and is now talking about saving up for a one bedroom apartment and a car for herself (she lives in a basement). She seems so sad but I cant help but feel like shes wrong for even asking me to not help my family. I dont know if I'm being an asshole or not for telling her that my family will always come first. AITA for telling her my family and their needs have to come before her and our future together?

This makes her feel **invisible and unimportant**. If you truly want to build a life with her, you need to **show her that she’s a priority**—not just in words, but in actions. - Right now, she feels like she’s **carrying the relationship alone**, while you’re focused on others. If you’re always prioritizing family over your own future, she may eventually feel like she’s **second to your responsibilities**—not as a partner, but as a **burden**. - Many couples in South Asia (and globally) balance family and love successfully, but it requires **clear communication and compromise**. Right now, you’re not compromising—you’re **defending an absolute priority** that leaves no room for her. 4. **Her reaction is valid—she’s scared.** - She’s not just angry; she’s **worried about her future**. If you keep saying family comes first, she may start to believe that **she’ll always be secondary**—and that’s a recipe for resentment or eventual separation. - Love isn’t just about emotional connection; it’s about **shared goals and security**. (0)** **No, not in the long term.** While your intentions (caring for family) are noble, **absolute prioritization without reciprocity is unhealthy for the relationship**. Here’s why it’s problematic: - **It creates an unequal dynamic.** She’s already working hard to support herself; if you’re not even saving for a future together, she may feel like she’s **alone in this**. - **It sets a precedent for future conflicts.** If you always put family first, she may later feel **replaced by your parents, siblings, or extended family**—especially when you have kids or face major life decisions. - **It ignores her needs as an equal partner.** A healthy relationship requires **both people to invest in the future**. The key is **balance**, not absolutes. - Example: Instead of saying *"Family always comes first,"* say: *"I love my family deeply, and I’ll always support them. But I also want to build a stable future with you. Right now, I’m trying to save for a down payment while still being there for them. Can we work together to make this happen?"* 2. **Show her through actions, not just words.** - If you’re serious about her, **start saving** (even if it’s small amounts). If you’re studying for your real estate license, **make time**—even if it means adjusting family expectations. - If she’s working hard to support herself, **help where you can** (e.g., offering to cover her rent occasionally, helping with bills, or contributing to her education). 3. **Have a serious conversation about her fears.** - Ask her: *"I love you, and I want us to have a future together. But I also feel torn between my family and us. How can I make you feel more secure that I’m committed to this?"* - Listen to her concerns—she’s not just being dramatic. She’s **worried about being left behind**. 4. **Consider compromises.** - Maybe you don’t have to **immediately** drop all family obligations, but you can **set boundaries** (e.g., *"I’ll be there for family events, but I also need to focus on saving for us"*). - If your mom’s settlement was unexpected, maybe you can **clarify with her** that while you’re grateful, you also need to plan for your own future. 5. **If she’s already planning for independence, it’s a red flag.** - The fact that she’s now talking about saving for her own apartment and car **without you** means she’s **starting to believe you won’t be there for her**. - This is a **relationship killer** in the long run. If you truly love her, you need to **show her that she’s your priority**—not just your family. --- ### **Final Verdict: You’re Wrong to Make It an Absolute.** Saying *"Family will always come before her"* is **emotionally damaging** because: - It makes her feel **unimportant**. - It sets up a **power imbalance** where she’s always second. - It **undermines trust** in the relationship. **The right approach is to balance both—care for your family *and* invest in her future.** If you can’t do that, the relationship will eventually **fail**, and she’ll move on to someone who **does** prioritize her.
